comparison: Perfect agreement on behavioral findings (C1-C3, C60-C61). Both evaluations find the behavioral evidence well-supported with appropriate statistics. OpenEval notes the interpretation is reasonable though causal mechanisms remain to be established; peer reviewers acknowledged the elegant design and rigorous conduct without questioning these behavioral claims.

Significant disagreement on visual response interpretation. OpenEval finds C4-C6, C20, C62 well-supported with robust statistics and appropriate controls. However, peer reviewers expressed serious concerns about the visual nature of responses (C4-C7, C19, C43-C44, C51, C77), stating 'the response of the authors has been insufficient to prove the visual nature of the evoked responses' and citing concerns about motor confounds and inconsistent latencies. Peer evaluation is UNCERTAIN while OpenEval is SUPPORTED.

Strong agreement on contralateral selectivity findings (C8-C13, C39-C41, C67-C68). Both evaluations find the selectivity patterns well-documented and consistent across experiments. OpenEval notes the critical test using left AC recordings provides strong evidence for learned associations; peer reviewers similarly accepted these findings as 'consistent across experiments and interpretable as a learned task-dependent effect.'

Agreement on enhanced selectivity and decoding findings (C17-C18, C64). Both evaluations accept the single-neuron selectivity and population decoding analyses. OpenEval finds the statistical comparisons appropriate and interpretation supported; peer reviewers noted the experiments were 'conducted in a rigorous manner' and did not challenge these temporal acceleration findings.

Strong agreement on pairing-specific integration (C21-C28, C49, C63). Both evaluations explicitly endorse these findings. OpenEval notes appropriate statistical tests and critical controls; peer reviewers stated 'The main result that multisensory interactions are specific for contralateral paired audiovisual stimuli is consistent across experiments' and praised the demonstration that active discrimination is necessary.

Both address correlation analysis (C29) but with different emphases. OpenEval (R6) evaluates C29-C30, C64 as SUPPORTED while noting correlation doesn't establish causation. Peer reviewers (R5) accepted C29 as part of the broader pairing-specific integration findings without specific concerns about the correlation analysis itself.

Agreement on subadditive integration characterization (C31). Both evaluations accept the bootstrap analysis and 83% quantification. OpenEval notes the methodology is sound but focuses on correct contralateral trials only; peer reviewers accepted this as part of the well-done analytical framework without challenge.

Disagreement on causal interpretation of MSI-behavior relationship (C32-C33, C71). OpenEval finds the statistical comparisons appropriate but notes the interpretation is speculative. Peer reviewers marked this UNCERTAIN, explicitly stating 'There are still parts of the manuscript that are inappropriately causal' and noting that high attention/motivation could explain both strong integration and good behavior.

Agreement on congruence effects and discrimination ability (C34-C38, C50, C65-C66, C79-C80). Both evaluations accept the matched vs. unmatched comparisons and population decoding results. OpenEval notes the interpretations are well-supported by data patterns; peer reviewers accepted that 'multisensory interactions were similarly specific for the congruent audiovisual pairing.'

Agreement on left AC findings (C42, C68). Both evaluations accept this as critical evidence for learned associations rather than stimulus properties. OpenEval praises the strong experimental design; peer reviewers noted that 'varying the recording hemisphere' strengthened findings and ruled out alternative explanations.

Strong agreement on unisensory training control (C43-C48, C69-C70). Both evaluations praise this as a critical experiment demonstrating training specificity. OpenEval notes the sharp contrast with multisensory-trained animals strongly supports interpretations; peer reviewers stated the comparisons were 'particularly thorough' and 'strengthen the authors' findings.'

Agreement on discrimination ability (C50-C52). OpenEval finds these summary claims well-documented but notes memory trace interpretation (C52) is inferential. Peer reviewers accepted the discrimination findings (C50) as part of the congruent pairing specificity without challenge.

Agreement on cited literature (C53-C59). Both evaluations accept these citations as appropriate context. OpenEval notes accuracy cannot be fully verified without checking sources; peer reviewers did not challenge the cited literature or its relevance to the findings.

Agreement that speculative claims are uncertain (C72-C76, C78). Both evaluations mark these as UNCERTAIN. OpenEval notes they extend beyond the data and require additional experiments; peer reviewers stated 'There are still parts of the manuscript that are inappropriately causal' and emphasized 'further work is needed to establish the origin and nature of these non-auditory signals.'

Both address timing/motor concerns (C77). OpenEval marks this UNCERTAIN, noting recent work shows rapid motor responses can occur within 50ms and movements weren't systematically tracked. Peer reviewers similarly expressed concerns about motor confounds in their UNCERTAIN evaluation of visual responses, with one stating 'it is still not possible to rule out motor effects completely.'

Agreement on SVM decoding analysis (C30). OpenEval finds this provides independent support for correlation findings; peer reviewers accepted decoding analyses as 'typically well done and properly address[ing] the questions raised' without specific challenge.

Different focus on training effects. OpenEval (R2) evaluates training enhancement of visual representation (C62) as SUPPORTED based on control group comparisons. Peer reviewers (R14) accepted this interpretation (C62) as SUPPORTED, noting comparisons show enhancements are 'dependent on learned associations in a task engaged state.'

Partial overlap on memory trace interpretation (C52). OpenEval notes this is inferential and would benefit from mechanistic studies. Peer reviewers similarly expressed concerns about mechanistic claims, stating 'further work is needed' to establish mechanisms definitively, marking related claims UNCERTAIN.

Minimal overlap on C19. OpenEval (R4) includes C19 in SUPPORTED evaluation of population decoding. Peer reviewers (R2) include C19 in their UNCERTAIN evaluation focused on visual response interpretation concerns, though they did not specifically challenge the decoding methodology itself.

Minimal overlap on C15. OpenEval (R3) includes C15 in SUPPORTED evaluation of contralateral preference. Peer reviewers (R11) include C15 in UNCERTAIN evaluation of mechanistic/causal claims, suggesting different interpretive emphasis on the same claim.
